name: Rationalism
statement: Reason, not sense experience, is the chief source and test of knowledge.
statementAccent: the chief source and test of knowledge
meaning: Rationalism is the epistemological view that reason is a primary source and test of knowledge, and that there are significant ways in which our concepts and knowledge are gained independently of sense experience, that is, a priori. Rationalists hold that reality has an inherently logical or intelligible structure that the intellect can grasp, and that reason can deliver substantive truths about the world, not merely trivial or verbal ones. The position is often analyzed into three theses, each relativized to a particular subject area. The Intuition and Deduction Thesis says that some propositions are knowable by rational intuition, a direct intellectual insight, and others by being deduced from intuited propositions. The Innate Knowledge Thesis says that we have knowledge of some truths as part of our rational nature, knowledge that experience may trigger but does not supply. The Innate Concept Thesis says that we possess some of our concepts, such as God, substance, or causation, innately, as part of our rational nature, with experience prompting rather than furnishing them. Rationalism is most associated with the great seventeenth-century Continental rationalists, Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz, and further back with Plato, and it stands in classic opposition to empiricism, which holds that knowledge comes from sense experience. The rationalism and empiricism dispute is central to early modern philosophy.
mechanism: Rationalism makes reason, rather than the senses, the fundamental source of substantive knowledge, and it does so through several claims. The core is the Intuition and Deduction Thesis: some truths are grasped directly by rational intuition, an intellectual seeing that a proposition is true, and further truths are reached by deducing them from these intuited starting points, as in mathematics, where axioms are intuited and theorems derived. This is why rationalists take mathematics and logic as models of knowledge and extend the method to metaphysics, ethics, and knowledge of the world. To explain how reason can know truths not given in experience, rationalists add the Innate Knowledge and Innate Concept theses: certain items of knowledge and certain concepts are part of our rational nature, latent within us, and experience serves only to trigger or awaken them rather than to create them, so a concept like causation or substance can outrun anything the senses could supply. Descartes deployed systematic doubt to reach the intuited certainty of his own existence and built outward by reason; Spinoza derived an entire philosophical system geometrically, in the Euclidean manner, from the idea of substance; Leibniz argued that necessary truths, such as those of mathematics, cannot come from experience, which shows only what is so, not what must be so, and so must have an innate, rational source. The mechanism throughout is the derivation of knowledge from reason and innate structure rather than from sensory input.

whyItMatters: Rationalism is one of the two great traditions in the theory of knowledge, the counterpart and rival to empiricism, and the dispute between them defines much of early modern philosophy. By holding that reason is a chief source of substantive knowledge and that some of our knowledge and concepts are gained independently of experience, rationalism poses the deep question of whether the mind can reach truths about reality by thought alone. The Continental rationalists, Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz, built some of the most ambitious systems in the history of philosophy on this conviction, taking mathematics as the model of certain knowledge and extending its method to God, mind, and world. Rationalism keeps alive the insight, pressed against strict empiricism, that necessary truths and the truths of mathematics and logic seem to be known a priori, not by observation, and that certain fundamental concepts may not be simply read off from the senses. The debate culminated in Kant's attempt to reconcile the two traditions through his notion of the synthetic a priori. As the view that reason is the primary source and test of knowledge, rationalism is a foundational position in epistemology and a permanent pole of the debate over the origins of human knowledge.

limits: Rationalism faces the standing challenge of empiricism and several specific difficulties. The central objection is to explain how pure reason could yield knowledge of the world rather than merely of the relations among our own ideas: if reason operates independently of experience, why should its deliverances match reality? Empiricists, from Locke to Hume, attacked the doctrine of innate ideas, arguing that the mind begins as a blank slate and that all our concepts derive ultimately from experience, and they charged that alleged rational insights are either trivial, true by the meanings of words, or unsupported. The problem of induction and the status of a priori knowledge became battlegrounds. Kant, seeking to reconcile the traditions, argued that rationalism overreached in claiming knowledge of things beyond possible experience while granting the rationalist that experience alone cannot account for the necessary, a priori structure of knowledge. The neat labels also oversimplify, since figures classed as rationalists or empiricists held mixed views. So rationalism robustly affirms reason as a source of substantive knowledge, understood as a major tradition challenged by empiricism over innate ideas and over how reason alone could know the world.
misreadings: Rationalism is not the claim that experience plays no role in knowledge at all; it is the claim that reason is a significant source of knowledge independent of experience, and most rationalists grant the senses some role. It is not merely a synonym for being reasonable or for valuing rationality in general, but a specific epistemological doctrine about the sources of knowledge. And it is not refuted simply by pointing to sensory knowledge, since its distinctive claims concern a priori and innate knowledge, so treating rationalism as denying experience entirely, as generic reasonableness, or as obviously false, misreads a foundational epistemological position.
origin: The epistemological tradition holding that reason is a chief source and test of knowledge and that some knowledge and concepts are gained independently of experience, associated with Plato and the Continental rationalists Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz.
